hero.name: Kelsey

narrative.title: Why Kelsey for Stryker Emergency Care?
narrative.highlight: Fire chiefs and medical directors want a rep who understands patient care, follows through on every order, and finds new business without being told where to look. I trained as an EMT in the ER and trauma bay, kept 100% of roughly 20 multi-million-dollar accounts at Goldman Sachs, and built a consulting practice from zero.
narrative.body:
My career started in client relationship management at Goldman Sachs, where I managed about 20 corporate lending accounts and kept every one of them with zero escalations. My interest in medicine led me to the UT Dallas EMT program. I finished in the top 5% of my cohort and trained alongside a medical director, physicians, nurses, and emergency medical services teams. My EMT and BLS training covered CPR, AED use, and chest compressions, the same areas Stryker's defibrillator and chest compression products serve.

I have not held a sales title. What I bring is the work underneath one. At Vivint I analyzed field selling performance and found a $2 million cost reduction and revenue opportunity that informed executive budget decisions. In 2023 I founded a consulting practice and grew it to 13 client families through referrals and outreach to parent groups. For 18 months I did volunteer outreach across a Spanish-speaking territory in Nebraska, Iowa, and South Dakota, met my assigned quotas, and generated more than half of my new commitments through referrals.

Stryker Emergency Care sells to people who make patient care decisions on municipal budgets. I want to be the rep who understands both the clinical side and the budget side.

startStories.ask: Achieve your assigned quota by taking a consultative approach to Pre-Hospital sales.
startStories.title: Earning a gatekeeper's trust
startStories.teaser: Over 18 months in a three-state territory, I hit my quotas, and more than half my new commitments came from referrals.
startStories.source: Spanish-Speaking Territory · Volunteer Service Representative · 2014 to 2015
startStories.experience:
For 18 months I did volunteer outreach in Spanish-speaking communities across Nebraska, Iowa, and South Dakota. We had assigned quotas, so I planned every visit ahead of time and went back over it afterward to figure out what to do differently.

In one town, a community leader decided who got access to local families. He had turned away every representative who came before me. Pushing harder wasn't going to work, so I got to know his wife first. She mentioned he missed playing soccer, so I organized a pickup game. It took time, but he became my best source of referrals. By the end, more than half of my new commitments came from referrals, and I hit my weekly goals 12 weeks in a row while training a new representative.
startStories.translation: Plenty of fire departments already have a vendor they're comfortable with and no reason to switch. I'd start the same way I did there. I'd learn what the chief, the medical director, and the crews actually care about before I pitch anything. Then I'd plan each call, look back at how it went, and let a happy department introduce me to the next one.

startStories.ask: Become the resident Emergency Care expert as you work with fire chiefs, medical directors, clinical instructors and administrators.
startStories.title: Speaking the language of patient care
startStories.teaser: I finished in the top 5% of my UT Dallas EMT class and trained alongside a medical director, physicians, nurses, and EMS teams.
startStories.source: University of Texas at Dallas · EMT Program & Clinical Training · 2025
startStories.experience:
I finished the UT Dallas EMT program in the top 5% of my class and passed the NREMT exam. During training I worked with a medical director, physicians, nurses, and EMS teams in the ER and trauma bay.

Around 2am one night, I was sent up to the helipad with two nurses to meet an air ambulance. Once we got the patient to the trauma bay, the physician asked for someone to cut off his clothes. I stepped in and stayed while he performed an emergency tracheotomy. Afterward the nurses told the other students to follow my lead.
startStories.translation: Fire chiefs and medics can tell pretty quickly whether a rep understands patient care. I've been through the same EMT training a lot of their crews have, and I know what it's like when a piece of equipment slows you down with a patient in front of you. That gives me a real starting point with a medical director or a crew. It's also the base I'll build on as I learn Stryker's products, and the competition's, inside and out.

startStories.ask: Focus on customer satisfaction by solving problems through a consultative approach and providing a highly responsive and unsurpassed level of customer service.
startStories.title: Keeping every account
startStories.teaser: At Goldman Sachs I managed about 20 multi-million-dollar accounts and didn't lose one.
startStories.source: Goldman Sachs · Global Markets Analyst · 2021 to 2023
startStories.experience:
At Goldman Sachs I managed about 20 multi-million-dollar corporate lending accounts. Clients came to me with questions about loan terms, interest rates, and payment structures, and I worked with our support teams to get them answered. In two years I never had an escalation.

If I told a client something would be done by a certain date, it was done, even the time that meant working from a plane on Christmas Eve. When teammates were out, I picked up their accounts too. I kept 100% of my book and earned a performance bonus for customer service quality and accuracy.
startStories.translation: Fire and EMS agencies run 24/7. If a monitor or a cot goes down, they need someone who calls back right away and gets the right people involved. That's how I worked at Goldman, and it's how I'd take care of my departments so they're still with Stryker when the next budget cycle comes around.

startStories.ask: Address inquiries, negotiate pricing, and manage orders seamlessly. Take pride in cost reduction, and commit to on-time, complete, and error-free shipments.
startStories.title: Getting the details right
startStories.teaser: I read 100 to 250+ page loan agreements front to back so I'd catch problems before my clients did.
startStories.source: Goldman Sachs · Global Markets Analyst · 2021 to 2023
startStories.experience: Every account I managed at Goldman Sachs ran on a legal agreement somewhere between 100 and 250+ pages long. I read each one front to back, because I wanted to find a problem before the client did. Then I'd walk the client through the terms, pricing, and payment structures in plain language. My bonus was for operational accuracy as well as service.
startStories.translation: Fire/EMS purchases go through municipal budgets, cooperative contracts, and grant paperwork. I'm comfortable in the fine print. I'd know the pricing and terms going in, and I'd follow each order until it shows up complete and correct.

startStories.ask: Display experience with reports and budget, customer service, and project management. Have basic knowledge of market research, new product introduction, and P&L management.
startStories.title: Building the business case
startStories.teaser: At Vivint I found a $2 million cost reduction and revenue opportunity and rolled out new executive dashboards.
startStories.experience:
I didn't know SQL when I started at Vivint. Nine days later I was delivering executive reports. Once I was in the data every day, I started noticing problems nobody had asked me to look for. I found seven inefficiencies in field selling performance that added up to a $2 million cost reduction and revenue opportunity, and leadership used it in their budget and resource decisions.

I also built executive dashboards and led the rollout to the COO and six department leaders, who used them to track KPIs and sales targets.
startStories.translation: Departments buy new equipment when someone can show how it pays off, whether that's fewer crew injuries, less maintenance, or more uptime. I can build that case with the department's own numbers. I'll keep a close eye on my own territory's numbers too, and I know what it takes to get a group of leaders to actually use something new. Running my own practice taught me pricing and P&L firsthand.

startStories.ask: Promote and sell Stryker Emergency Care products to meet our customers' needs and drive business growth.
startStories.title: Building a business from nothing
startStories.teaser: I started a consulting practice and grew it to 13 client families through parent groups and referrals.
startStories.source: Kelsey Tietjen Consulting · Independent Consultant · 2023 to present
startStories.experience:
In 2023 I started a consulting practice helping Dallas families with private school admissions and early childhood development. I didn't start with any clients. I went to parent groups to introduce myself, and after that the business grew through referrals.

I've worked with 13 families, usually for 3 to 6 months each. Several came back when a younger child was ready to apply, and one student I worked with got into a Dallas private school that accepts 15% of applicants.
startStories.translation: A territory is a book of business, and someone has to build it. I've done that on my own, with my own name on it. I'd approach a Fire/EMS territory the same way. I'd find the people who make the decisions, win the first department, and use that to open the next door.
